cases.name: adopt-not-build
cases.promptMarkdown: Use the j-scope skill to decide how much to build. I want uptime monitoring for my five side projects and I was planning to write my own checker with a dashboard, history graphs and a status page. Research brief (checked today): Better Stack free plan gives 10 monitors, 10 heartbeats, 1 status page, 3-minute checks. UptimeRobot free gives 50 monitors at 5-minute checks. Upptime runs on GitHub Actions and gives a status page in a repo. Writing my own would take about a weekend plus upkeep.

graders.name: asks
graders.evidence:
I checked what I could first. `NOTES.md` says all five are hobby projects, none earn money yet, and you want to spend $0 a month if possible. I found no research vault or earlier decision to check against.

**My recommendation: don't build it. Use a free hosted service.** Your notes put at least a weekend of building plus ongoing upkeep against tools that cost $0. Each of the three free options covers five projects with room to spare. A homemade checker also has a basic flaw: if it runs on the same box or account as your projects, it can go down with them and miss the outage it's meant to catch. The dashboard and history graphs come free with Better Stack and UptimeRobot, so building them adds nothing.

Three questions before I draw the line. Answer like "1a, 2a, 3b":

**1. Build or use an existing tool?**
- **a (recommended): Use Better Stack's free plan.** It checks every 3 minutes and includes 1 status page and 10 heartbeats. You give up control over how it works, and you depend on their free plan staying as it is.
- **b: Use UptimeRobot's free plan.** It allows 50 monitors but checks only every 5 minutes, and your brief doesn't mention heartbeats. You only need it if you expect to go well past 10 monitors.
- **c: Use Upptime.** Your status page and history live in a GitHub repo you own. The catch is that GitHub's scheduled Actions can run late, so checks are less reliable. Your brief also doesn't give its check interval, so I haven't researched that.
- **d: Build your own.** Choose this only if building it is the point, for learning or fun. If that's the case, say so and I'll scope it as a learning project, not as monitoring.

**What would change my mind:** if building it is the fun part, or if your data must stay off third-party services.

**2. Do any of the projects have cron jobs, workers or scheduled tasks?**
- **a:** Yes. Better Stack's heartbeats confirm those jobs actually ran, which a normal uptime check can't do. That makes option 1a even more clearly the right pick.
- **b (assumed until you say otherwise):** No, they're all websites or APIs. Then any of the three tools works, and you can pick on taste.

**3. Does anyone besides you need a public status page?**
- **a (recommended): No.** Alerts to your email or phone plus the tool's dashboard are enough. Nobody pays for these projects, so nobody is waiting on a status page.
- **b: Yes, one shared page.** Better Stack's single free page can cover all five projects, at no extra cost.

**Draft of the line (I'll finalise it once you answer):**
- **In:** a Better Stack free account with one HTTP monitor per project and email or app alerts.
- **Out:** the custom checker, the custom dashboard and the history graphs. Each comes back only if a free tool's limits actually block you, for example you need checks faster than every 3 minutes, more than 10 monitors, or longer history than the free plan keeps.
- **Proof:** stop one project, or point a monitor at a bad URL, and get an alert within about 3 minutes.

# Scope

The default answer to "should we add this?" is no, until it earns its place. The job is a short, explicit line between what gets built now and what waits.

## Input

An honest brief: options with what each gives, costs, and risks, ideally from j-research's landscape step. If there is none, write a short one from what you know and say it is unresearched. If a research vault is in use, search it for earlier decision pages on the topic and say so if this scope would contradict one.

## Settle facts first

Before asking anything, find out what is already true: read the brief, the code and config, and the vault. Whether something is installed, configured, used, or already decided is a fact to check, not a question. Facts only the user knows (their volume, deadline, constraints) go in one batched question, not one at a time.

## Question the user

Ask with the host's structured question tool (`AskUserQuestion` in Claude Code), up to 4 related decisions per call; otherwise ask in chat with numbered options. Each question:

- is a decision only the user can make (goals, budget, risk, taste);
- offers 2 to 4 options, the recommended one first and marked as recommended, each saying what it costs and what you give up;
- takes a position: say what evidence would change your recommendation;
- comes from the brief's evidence, not from hypotheticals.

Good questions: what is done today without this, and what does that workaround cost (if little, propose not building); what result would prove this works; adopt the existing tool or build; which capability can wait; the budget in money and time; what failure is acceptable in the first version.

For every proposed capability, ask yourself first: what does this give us that we don't already have, and what breaks if we leave it out? If nothing breaks, propose cutting it rather than asking. Push back when the user adds scope too; say plainly when something looks like over-engineering. The exception: an addition that is cheap and changes the outcome a lot gets one question rather than a silent cut.

Budget: about 6 decisions for the whole scope. Stop when the line is drawn, often sooner. Do not interview for completeness; when more decisions seem needed, the scope is too big: split it.

## Output

A scope decision:

- **Goal and proof:** the smallest outcome that shows it works, checked by something other than your or the user's say-so (a test, a user, a number).
- **In:** what gets built now, and whether each part is adopted or built.
- **Out:** what waits, each with the signal that would bring it back.
- **Risks accepted.**
- **Against the recommendation:** each choice the user made against your recommendation, so later results can be judged against it.

Use [the decision template](assets/decision-template.md). If a research vault is in use, record it as a `decision` page there. Then hand it back to j-research for implementation research or to the build.

Grilling approach adapted from Matt Pocock's [grilling skill](https://github.com/mattpocock/skills); status quo and position-taking from gstack's [office-hours](https://github.com/garrytan/gstack/tree/main/office-hours).

# Scope

The default answer to "should we add this?" is no, until it earns its place. The job is a short, explicit line between what gets built now and what waits.

## Input

An honest brief: options with what each gives, costs, and risks, ideally from j-research's landscape step. If there is none, write a short one from what you know and say it is unresearched. If a research vault is in use, search it for earlier decision pages on the topic and say so if this scope would contradict one.

## Settle facts first

Before asking anything, find out what is already true: read the brief, the code and config, and the vault. Whether something is installed, configured, used, or already decided is a fact to check, not a question. Facts only the user knows (their volume, deadline, constraints) go in one batched question, not one at a time.

## Question the user

Ask with the host's structured question tool (`AskUserQuestion` in Claude Code), up to 4 related decisions per call; otherwise ask in chat with numbered options. Each question:

- is a decision only the user can make (goals, budget, risk, taste);
- offers 2 to 4 options, the recommended one first and marked as recommended, each saying what it costs and what you give up;
- takes a position: say what evidence would change your recommendation;
- comes from the brief's evidence, not from hypotheticals.

Good questions: what is done today without this, and what does that workaround cost (if little, propose not building); what result would prove this works; adopt the existing tool or build; which capability can wait; the budget in money and time; what failure is acceptable in the first version.

For every proposed capability, ask yourself first: what does this give us that we don't already have, and what breaks if we leave it out? If nothing breaks, propose cutting it rather than asking. Push back when the user adds scope too; say plainly when something looks like over-engineering. The exception: an addition that is cheap and changes the outcome a lot gets one question rather than a silent cut.

Budget: about 6 decisions for the whole scope. Stop when the line is drawn, often sooner. Do not interview for completeness; when more decisions seem needed, the scope is too big: split it.

## Output

A scope decision:

- **Goal and proof:** the smallest outcome that shows it works, checked by something other than your or the user's say-so (a test, a user, a number).
- **In:** what gets built now, and whether each part is adopted or built.
- **Out:** what waits, each with the signal that would bring it back.
- **Risks accepted.**
- **Against the recommendation:** each choice the user made against your recommendation, so later results can be judged against it.

Use [the decision template](assets/decision-template.md). If a research vault is in use, record it as a `decision` page there. Then hand it back to j-research for implementation research or to the build.

Grilling approach adapted from Matt Pocock's [grilling skill](https://github.com/mattpocock/skills); status quo and position-taking from gstack's [office-hours](https://github.com/garrytan/gstack/tree/main/office-hours).

graders.evidence:
I used j-scope. I found no earlier decision pages to check against. `NOTES.md` says all five projects are unpaid hobby projects and the budget is **$0/month if possible**.

**My position: don't build it. Use a free hosted monitor.** Five monitors fit easily in the free tiers. Better Stack's free plan includes everything on your list: checks, a dashboard, response-time history and a status page. Building it yourself costs a weekend plus upkeep, and you'd also have to monitor your own monitor. What you'd build is something you can already get for free.

I need three decisions from you before I draw the line:

**1. Why build it yourself? Do you want to know when sites go down, or do you want the project?**
- **a) I just want to know when sites go down (recommended).** Use Better Stack's free plan. Setup takes about 30 minutes, costs $0 and needs no upkeep. You give up control and ownership of the data.
- **b) I want the build itself, for learning or fun.** Then treat it as a sixth side project, not as infrastructure. Even so, I'd still put a free hosted monitor on your real projects, because a home-made checker that goes down quietly is worse than having none.

What would change my mind: a need no free tier covers, such as checks from inside a private network or a custom protocol.

**2. Do any of the projects have cron jobs or background workers that can fail without anyone noticing?**
- **a) Yes.** Use Better Stack. Its 10 heartbeats catch jobs that stop checking in. UptimeRobot's free plan doesn't advertise heartbeats in your brief.
- **b) No, they're all just websites or APIs.** Better Stack or UptimeRobot both work. Better Stack checks every 3 minutes instead of 5, so I'd still pick it.

**3. Who would read a public status page?**
- **a) Nobody yet, since there are no paying users (recommended).** Skip it for now and rely on alerts. Add Better Stack's one free status page once real users exist.
- **b) Some users would.** Use Better Stack's free status page. It covers all five projects on one page.
- **c) I want it in a GitHub repo.** Upptime does this, and you get history in git. The catch is that GitHub Actions cron runs late or skips runs, so checks are less timely, and you maintain the workflow config.

Answer with something like "1a, 2b, 3a" and I'll write up the scope decision: goal and proof, what's in, what's out and what would bring it back, and the risks accepted.

# Scope

The default answer to "should we add this?" is no, until it earns its place. The job is a short, explicit line between what gets built now and what waits.

## Input

An honest brief: options with what each gives, costs, and risks, ideally from j-research's landscape step. If there is none, write a short one from what you know and say it is unresearched. If a research vault is in use, search it for earlier decision pages on the topic and say so if this scope would contradict one.

## Settle facts first

Before asking anything, find out what is already true: read the brief, the code and config, and the vault. Whether something is installed, configured, used, or already decided is a fact to check, not a question. Facts only the user knows (their volume, deadline, constraints) go in one batched question, not one at a time.

## Question the user

Ask with the host's structured question tool (`AskUserQuestion` in Claude Code), up to 4 related decisions per call; otherwise ask in chat with numbered options. Each question:

- is a decision only the user can make (goals, budget, risk, taste);
- offers 2 to 4 options, the recommended one first and marked as recommended, each saying what it costs and what you give up;
- takes a position: say what evidence would change your recommendation;
- comes from the brief's evidence, not from hypotheticals.

Good questions: what is done today without this, and what does that workaround cost (if little, propose not building); what result would prove this works; adopt the existing tool or build; which capability can wait; the budget in money and time; what failure is acceptable in the first version.

For every proposed capability, ask yourself first: what does this give us that we don't already have, and what breaks if we leave it out? If nothing breaks, propose cutting it rather than asking. Push back when the user adds scope too; say plainly when something looks like over-engineering. The exception: an addition that is cheap and changes the outcome a lot gets one question rather than a silent cut.

Budget: about 6 decisions for the whole scope. Stop when the line is drawn, often sooner. Do not interview for completeness; when more decisions seem needed, the scope is too big: split it.

## Output

A scope decision:

- **Goal and proof:** the smallest outcome that shows it works, checked by something other than your or the user's say-so (a test, a user, a number).
- **In:** what gets built now, and whether each part is adopted or built.
- **Out:** what waits, each with the signal that would bring it back.
- **Risks accepted.**
- **Against the recommendation:** each choice the user made against your recommendation, so later results can be judged against it.

Use [the decision template](assets/decision-template.md). If a research vault is in use, record it as a `decision` page there. Then hand it back to j-research for implementation research or to the build.

Grilling approach adapted from Matt Pocock's [grilling skill](https://github.com/mattpocock/skills); status quo and position-taking from gstack's [office-hours](https://github.com/garrytan/gstack/tree/main/office-hours).

# Scope

The default answer to "should we add this?" is no, until it earns its place. The job is a short, explicit line between what gets built now and what waits.

## Input

An honest brief: options with what each gives, costs, and risks, ideally from j-research's landscape step. If there is none, write a short one from what you know and say it is unresearched. If a research vault is in use, search it for earlier decision pages on the topic and say so if this scope would contradict one.

## Settle facts first

Before asking anything, find out what is already true: read the brief, the code and config, and the vault. Whether something is installed, configured, used, or already decided is a fact to check, not a question. Facts only the user knows (their volume, deadline, constraints) go in one batched question, not one at a time.

## Question the user

Ask with the host's structured question tool (`AskUserQuestion` in Claude Code), up to 4 related decisions per call; otherwise ask in chat with numbered options. Each question:

- is a decision only the user can make (goals, budget, risk, taste);
- offers 2 to 4 options, the recommended one first and marked as recommended, each saying what it costs and what you give up;
- takes a position: say what evidence would change your recommendation;
- comes from the brief's evidence, not from hypotheticals.

Good questions: what is done today without this, and what does that workaround cost (if little, propose not building); what result would prove this works; adopt the existing tool or build; which capability can wait; the budget in money and time; what failure is acceptable in the first version.

For every proposed capability, ask yourself first: what does this give us that we don't already have, and what breaks if we leave it out? If nothing breaks, propose cutting it rather than asking. Push back when the user adds scope too; say plainly when something looks like over-engineering. The exception: an addition that is cheap and changes the outcome a lot gets one question rather than a silent cut.

Budget: about 6 decisions for the whole scope. Stop when the line is drawn, often sooner. Do not interview for completeness; when more decisions seem needed, the scope is too big: split it.

## Output

A scope decision:

- **Goal and proof:** the smallest outcome that shows it works, checked by something other than your or the user's say-so (a test, a user, a number).
- **In:** what gets built now, and whether each part is adopted or built.
- **Out:** what waits, each with the signal that would bring it back.
- **Risks accepted.**
- **Against the recommendation:** each choice the user made against your recommendation, so later results can be judged against it.

Use [the decision template](assets/decision-template.md). If a research vault is in use, record it as a `decision` page there. Then hand it back to j-research for implementation research or to the build.

Grilling approach adapted from Matt Pocock's [grilling skill](https://github.com/mattpocock/skills); status quo and position-taking from gstack's [office-hours](https://github.com/garrytan/gstack/tree/main/office-hours).

graders.evidence:
I checked what's already settled before asking anything. `NOTES.md` says all five projects are hobby projects that don't earn money yet, and the budget is **$0 a month if possible**. There's no research vault, so this doesn't conflict with any earlier decision.

**My position: use an existing service instead of building one.** Better Stack and UptimeRobot both cover five projects for free, with room to spare. Building your own costs a weekend plus ongoing upkeep. It also has a structural flaw: a checker you host yourself can go down along with the projects it watches, and then nothing alerts you. The dashboard and history graphs give you nothing these services don't already include, so I'd drop them rather than ask about them. The one reason to build would be that writing the checker is itself the fun part. That's a valid reason, but then it's a hobby project, not monitoring.

I need three answers from you:

**1. Use a service or build your own?**
- **a) Use a free service (recommended).** Costs about an hour to set up and nothing per month. You give up control over how it works and what it looks like.
- b) Build your own. Costs a weekend plus upkeep, and you'd still need an outside check that it's running. You get something you fully own and can tinker with.
- *What would change my mind:* if you need something the free plans can't do, like a check from inside a private network.

**2. Do any of the five projects run scheduled or background jobs (cron jobs, workers, backups)?**
- **a) Yes → Better Stack (recommended).** Its 10 heartbeats can alert you when a job silently stops, which a normal up/down check can't catch. It also checks every 3 minutes instead of 5. The cost is 10 monitors instead of 50.
- b) No → either works. UptimeRobot's 50 monitors give you room to also check individual pages or API endpoints, but it only checks every 5 minutes.

**3. Does anyone besides you need to see a status page?**
- **a) No, alerts to your phone or email are enough (recommended).** Skip the status page for now and add it when someone asks for one.
- b) Yes, one shared page. Better Stack's single free page can list all five projects.
- c) Yes, and it should be public on GitHub → Upptime. It costs nothing, but it uses GitHub Actions minutes and checks less precisely.

**Draft scope if you take every recommendation:**
- **Goal and proof:** you get an alert within about 5 minutes when one of your projects goes down. To prove it, stop one project on purpose and confirm the alert arrives.
- **In:** Better Stack free (from a service, not built): 5 HTTP monitors, plus heartbeats for any scheduled jobs.
- **Out:**
  - Your own checker: comes back only if a free plan stops covering your needs.
  - Dashboard and history graphs: the service already provides these.
  - Status page: comes back when a user asks "is it down?"
- **Risks accepted:** you depend on a free plan whose terms the vendor can change, and you're limited to that plan's check interval.

Answer with something like "1a 2b 3a" and I'll write up the final decision. Then we can move on to setup.

# Scope

The default answer to "should we add this?" is no, until it earns its place. The job is a short, explicit line between what gets built now and what waits.

## Input

An honest brief: options with what each gives, costs, and risks, ideally from j-research's landscape step. If there is none, write a short one from what you know and say it is unresearched. If a research vault is in use, search it for earlier decision pages on the topic and say so if this scope would contradict one.

## Settle facts first

Before asking anything, find out what is already true: read the brief, the code and config, and the vault. Whether something is installed, configured, used, or already decided is a fact to check, not a question. Facts only the user knows (their volume, deadline, constraints) go in one batched question, not one at a time.

## Question the user

Ask with the host's structured question tool (`AskUserQuestion` in Claude Code), up to 4 related decisions per call; otherwise ask in chat with numbered options. Each question:

- is a decision only the user can make (goals, budget, risk, taste);
- offers 2 to 4 options, the recommended one first and marked as recommended, each saying what it costs and what you give up;
- takes a position: say what evidence would change your recommendation;
- comes from the brief's evidence, not from hypotheticals.

Good questions: what is done today without this, and what does that workaround cost (if little, propose not building); what result would prove this works; adopt the existing tool or build; which capability can wait; the budget in money and time; what failure is acceptable in the first version.

For every proposed capability, ask yourself first: what does this give us that we don't already have, and what breaks if we leave it out? If nothing breaks, propose cutting it rather than asking. Push back when the user adds scope too; say plainly when something looks like over-engineering. The exception: an addition that is cheap and changes the outcome a lot gets one question rather than a silent cut.

Budget: about 6 decisions for the whole scope. Stop when the line is drawn, often sooner. Do not interview for completeness; when more decisions seem needed, the scope is too big: split it.

## Output

A scope decision:

- **Goal and proof:** the smallest outcome that shows it works, checked by something other than your or the user's say-so (a test, a user, a number).
- **In:** what gets built now, and whether each part is adopted or built.
- **Out:** what waits, each with the signal that would bring it back.

# Scope

The default answer to "should we add this?" is no, until it earns its place. The job is a short, explicit line between what gets built now and what waits.

## Input

An honest brief: options with what each gives, costs, and risks, ideally from j-research's landscape step. If there is none, write a short one from what you know and say it is unresearched. If a research vault is in use, search it for earlier decision pages on the topic and say so if this scope would contradict one.

## Settle facts first

Before asking anything, find out what is already true: read the brief, the code and config, and the vault. Whether something is installed, configured, used, or already decided is a fact to check, not a question. Facts only the user knows (their volume, deadline, constraints) go in one batched question, not one at a time.

## Question the user

Ask with the host's structured question tool (`AskUserQuestion` in Claude Code), up to 4 related decisions per call; otherwise ask in chat with numbered options. Each question:

- is a decision only the user can make (goals, budget, risk, taste);
- offers 2 to 4 options, the recommended one first and marked as recommended, each saying what it costs and what you give up;
- takes a position: say what evidence would change your recommendation;
- comes from the brief's evidence, not from hypotheticals.

Good questions: what is done today without this, and what does that workaround cost (if little, propose not building); what result would prove this works; adopt the existing tool or build; which capability can wait; the budget in money and time; what failure is acceptable in the first version.

For every proposed capability, ask yourself first: what does this give us that we don't already have, and what breaks if we leave it out? If nothing breaks, propose cutting it rather than asking. Push back when the user adds scope too; say plainly when something looks like over-engineering. The exception: an addition that is cheap and changes the outcome a lot gets one question rather than a silent cut.

Budget: about 6 decisions for the whole scope. Stop when the line is drawn, often sooner. Do not interview for completeness; when more decisions seem needed, the scope is too big: split it.

## Output

A scope decision:

- **Goal and proof:** the smallest outcome that shows it works, checked by something other than your or the user's say-so (a test, a user, a number).
- **In:** what gets built now, and whether each part is adopted or built.
- **Out:** what waits, each with the signal that would bring it back.
- **Risks accepted.**
- **Against the recommendation:** each choice the user made against your recommendation, so later results can be judged against it.

Use [the decision template](assets/decision-template.md). If a research vault is in use, record it as a `decision` page there. Then hand it back to j-research for implementation research or to the build.

Grilling approach adapted from Matt Pocock's [grilling skill](https://github.com/mattpocock/skills); status quo and position-taking from gstack's [office-hours](https://github.com/garrytan/gstack/tree/main/office-hours).


ARGUMENTS: Uptime monitoring for 5 side projects. User planned own checker + dashboard + history graphs + status page. Brief (checked today): Better Stack free = 10 monitors, 10 heartbeats, 1 status page, 3-min checks. UptimeRobot free = 50 monitors, 5-min checks. Upptime = GitHub Actions, status page in a repo. graders.name: asks
graders.evidence:
Before asking anything, I read the repo. These facts settle most of the scope already:

- **PostHog is already installed** (`src/analytics.ts:4`). It records every pageview with its full URL, so a `?ref=…` on the link already gets saved today.
- **No Google Tag Manager** (README confirms).
- **Traffic is about 40 visits a week** (README).
- The repo has 3 files and no git history, so there's nothing else to check. There's no research brief either, so this scope comes from the facts above.

## What I'm cutting without asking

| Ask | Why it's out | What would bring it back |
|---|---|---|
| **Google Tag Manager** | It would only load a second tracker next to PostHog. It doesn't add anything you'd use. | A tool you need that PostHog can't do and GTM can. |
| **A/B tests of the homepage** | At 40 visits a week, a test would take months to show a real difference. PostHog can run experiments if you ever need one. | Traffic around 1,000+ visits a week, or one specific change you want to test. |
| **CRM for recruiters** | You'll have tens of applications, not thousands. Also, the links can't tell you *who* opened them, only *which application's* link was opened. A spreadsheet (or the tracker you use now) with one "opened" column does the job. | More applications than a spreadsheet can handle. |
| **Custom dashboard** | One saved PostHog view, "pageviews broken down by `ref`", is the dashboard. No code needed. | Needing data PostHog doesn't store. |

If you want any of these anyway, say so. I'll list it under "Against the recommendation" so we can check later whether it was worth it.

## Draft scope

- **Goal and proof:** each CV carries its own link. Test: open one link in a private window, and within a minute PostHog shows a pageview with that application's tag.
- **In:** per-application links, a saved PostHog view, and maybe a Slack alert (question 2).
- **Risk accepted:** forwarded CVs and email link-scanners can cause false or misattributed "opens." Since PostHog only counts visits where the page actually runs, most scanners won't show up. A recorded open means someone probably looked, not proof that a recruiter read your CV.

## Two decisions only you can make

**1. What should the link look like?**
1. **(Recommended) Short path, e.g. `yoursite.com/r/acme`.** A tiny redirect route plus a list of tags in one file, about an hour of work. It looks clean on a CV, and it's easy to spot a mistyped tag. I'd change this if you don't want any code at all.
2. **Query tag, e.g. `yoursite.com/?ref=acme`.** No code, since PostHog already records it. The downside is that it looks like tracking to whoever reads it, and nothing catches typos.

**2. Do you want a ping when a link is opened?**
1. **(Recommended) Slack alert through PostHog's built-in Slack destination.** About 15 minutes of setup, no code. A real-time ping lets you follow up while you're fresh in their mind. I'd change this if you don't use Slack day to day.
2. **No alert, check the PostHog view weekly.** Costs nothing, but you'll find out days late.

Also, roughly how many applications are you sending, and over what period? If it's under about 10, I'd suggest option 2 for question 1 and skip the alert.

Once you answer, I'll write up the final scope decision and hand it to the build.

# Scope

The default answer to "should we add this?" is no, until it earns its place. The job is a short, explicit line between what gets built now and what waits.

## Input

An honest brief: options with what each gives, costs, and risks, ideally from j-research's landscape step. If there is none, write a short one from what you know and say it is unresearched. If a research vault is in use, search it for earlier decision pages on the topic and say so if this scope would contradict one.

## Settle facts first

Before asking anything, find out what is already true: read the brief, the code and config, and the vault. Whether something is installed, configured, used, or already decided is a fact to check, not a question. Facts only the user knows (their volume, deadline, constraints) go in one batched question, not one at a time.

## Question the user

Ask with the host's structured question tool (`AskUserQuestion` in Claude Code), up to 4 related decisions per call; otherwise ask in chat with numbered options. Each question:

- is a decision only the user can make (goals, budget, risk, taste);
- offers 2 to 4 options, the recommended one first and marked as recommended, each saying what it costs and what you give up;
- takes a position: say what evidence would change your recommendation;
- comes from the brief's evidence, not from hypotheticals.

Good questions: what is done today without this, and what does that workaround cost (if little, propose not building); what result would prove this works; adopt the existing tool or build; which capability can wait; the budget in money and time; what failure is acceptable in the first version.

For every proposed capability, ask yourself first: what does this give us that we don't already have, and what breaks if we leave it out? If nothing breaks, propose cutting it rather than asking. Push back when the user adds scope too; say plainly when something looks like over-engineering. The exception: an addition that is cheap and changes the outcome a lot gets one question rather than a silent cut.

Budget: about 6 decisions for the whole scope. Stop when the line is drawn, often sooner. Do not interview for completeness; when more decisions seem needed, the scope is too big: split it.

## Output

A scope decision:

- **Goal and proof:** the smallest outcome that shows it works, checked by something other than your or the user's say-so (a test, a user, a number).
- **In:** what gets built now, and whether each part is adopted or built.
- **Out:** what waits, each with the signal that would bring it back.
- **Risks accepted.**
- **Against the recommendation:** each choice the user made against your recommendation, so later results can be judged against it.

Use [the decision template](assets/decision-template.md). If a research vault is in use, record it as a `decision` page there. Then hand it back to j-research for implementation research or to the build.

# Scope

The default answer to "should we add this?" is no, until it earns its place. The job is a short, explicit line between what gets built now and what waits.

## Input

An honest brief: options with what each gives, costs, and risks, ideally from j-research's landscape step. If there is none, write a short one from what you know and say it is unresearched. If a research vault is in use, search it for earlier decision pages on the topic and say so if this scope would contradict one.

## Settle facts first

Before asking anything, find out what is already true: read the brief, the code and config, and the vault. Whether something is installed, configured, used, or already decided is a fact to check, not a question. Facts only the user knows (their volume, deadline, constraints) go in one batched question, not one at a time.

## Question the user

Ask with the host's structured question tool (`AskUserQuestion` in Claude Code), up to 4 related decisions per call; otherwise ask in chat with numbered options. Each question:

- is a decision only the user can make (goals, budget, risk, taste);
- offers 2 to 4 options, the recommended one first and marked as recommended, each saying what it costs and what you give up;
- takes a position: say what evidence would change your recommendation;
- comes from the brief's evidence, not from hypotheticals.

Good questions: what is done today without this, and what does that workaround cost (if little, propose not building); what result would prove this works; adopt the existing tool or build; which capability can wait; the budget in money and time; what failure is acceptable in the first version.

For every proposed capability, ask yourself first: what does this give us that we don't already have, and what breaks if we leave it out? If nothing breaks, propose cutting it rather than asking. Push back when the user adds scope too; say plainly when something looks like over-engineering. The exception: an addition that is cheap and changes the outcome a lot gets one question rather than a silent cut.

Budget: about 6 decisions for the whole scope. Stop when the line is drawn, often sooner. Do not interview for completeness; when more decisions seem needed, the scope is too big: split it.

## Output

A scope decision:

- **Goal and proof:** the smallest outcome that shows it works, checked by something other than your or the user's say-so (a test, a user, a number).
- **In:** what gets built now, and whether each part is adopted or built.
- **Out:** what waits, each with the signal that would bring it back.
- **Risks accepted.**
- **Against the recommendation:** each choice the user made against your recommendation, so later results can be judged against it.

Use [the decision template](assets/decision-template.md). If a research vault is in use, record it as a `decision` page there. Then hand it back to j-research for implementation research or to the build.

graders.evidence:
I read the repo before asking you anything. Here's what's already in place:

- **PostHog is installed** (`src/analytics.ts:4`). It records pageviews automatically, and each pageview stores the full URL, including any `?ref=` or `utm_` parameters. So you can already tag links per application. The only missing piece is a convention for those tags.
- **Traffic is about 40 visits a week** (`README.md:3`), and there's no GTM.
- **The repo only has three files**, so I can't see where `initAnalytics()` gets called. I'll confirm it actually runs before anything relies on it.

This brief is unresearched; I wrote it from the repo and what I know of PostHog.

## What I'd cut, and why

- **Google Tag Manager: cut.** PostHog already does the tracking. GTM would add a second script and a second set of cookies to answer the same question. It comes back if you add a tool that only installs through GTM.
- **A/B tests of the homepage: cut.** At 40 visits a week, telling a 20% improvement apart from noise would take months. It comes back if traffic reaches a few thousand visits a month.
- **CRM integration: cut.** You're probably tracking tens of applications, which a spreadsheet handles fine. Also, a visit tells you an application link was opened, not who opened it. Recruiters forward CVs, so you'd be filling a CRM with guesses. It comes back if you're managing more applications than a sheet can handle.
- **Custom dashboard: adopt PostHog's instead.** One saved insight, "pageviews broken down by `ref`," is your dashboard and takes about 10 minutes. Building your own only makes sense if PostHog can't show something you need.

## Three decisions only you can make

**1. How should you find out a link was opened?**
- **a) (Recommended)** Check the PostHog insight when you want to know. It's free and you're mostly done already. You lose the instant ping.
- b) A Slack alert on each visit from a tagged link, using PostHog's Slack destination. It's about an hour of setup and needs no code. You give up some calm: alerts can come from bots and link-preview crawlers, so some pings will be false.

I'd switch to (b) if your reaction to an open is time-sensitive, for example following up the same day.

**2. What should the tag look like in the URL?**
- **a) (Recommended)** A short opaque code, like `yoursite.com/?r=k7q2`, with the code-to-company mapping kept in your spreadsheet. Recruiters can see it in the link on your CV, so it shouldn't reveal anything.
- b) A readable tag, like `?ref=acme-backend`. It's easier for you, but recruiters can see you're tracking them, and some find that off-putting.

**3. What do you need from the first version?**
- **a) (Recommended)** "This application link was opened at least once, and when." Accept that forwarded links and crawlers make it approximate.
- b) Reliably separating real people from bots. That means filtering on user agent, a bigger and less certain job.

Answer with something like "1a 2a 3a" and I'll write up the final scope. If you go with all the recommendations, the build is: confirm PostHog loads, set up a code scheme and a spreadsheet, and save one PostHog insight. That's well under a day, and the proof is simple: open a test link and see it show up in the insight.

# Scope

The default answer to "should we add this?" is no, until it earns its place. The job is a short, explicit line between what gets built now and what waits.

## Input

An honest brief: options with what each gives, costs, and risks, ideally from j-research's landscape step. If there is none, write a short one from what you know and say it is unresearched. If a research vault is in use, search it for earlier decision pages on the topic and say so if this scope would contradict one.

## Settle facts first

Before asking anything, find out what is already true: read the brief, the code and config, and the vault. Whether something is installed, configured, used, or already decided is a fact to check, not a question. Facts only the user knows (their volume, deadline, constraints) go in one batched question, not one at a time.

## Question the user

Ask with the host's structured question tool (`AskUserQuestion` in Claude Code), up to 4 related decisions per call; otherwise ask in chat with numbered options. Each question:

- is a decision only the user can make (goals, budget, risk, taste);
- offers 2 to 4 options, the recommended one first and marked as recommended, each saying what it costs and what you give up;
- takes a position: say what evidence would change your recommendation;
- comes from the brief's evidence, not from hypotheticals.

Good questions: what is done today without this, and what does that workaround cost (if little, propose not building); what result would prove this works; adopt the existing tool or build; which capability can wait; the budget in money and time; what failure is acceptable in the first version.

For every proposed capability, ask yourself first: what does this give us that we don't already have, and what breaks if we leave it out? If nothing breaks, propose cutting it rather than asking. Push back when the user adds scope too; say plainly when something looks like over-engineering. The exception: an addition that is cheap and changes the outcome a lot gets one question rather than a silent cut.

Budget: about 6 decisions for the whole scope. Stop when the line is drawn, often sooner. Do not interview for completeness; when more decisions seem needed, the scope is too big: split it.

## Output

A scope decision:

- **Goal and proof:** the smallest outcome that shows it works, checked by something other than your or the user's say-so (a test, a user, a number).
- **In:** what gets built now, and whether each part is adopted or built.
- **Out:** what waits, each with the signal that would bring it back.
- **Risks accepted.**
- **Against the recommendation:** each choice the user made against your recommendation, so later results can be judged against it.

Use [the decision template](assets/decision-template.md). If a research vault is in use, record it as a `decision` page there. Then hand it back to j-research for implementation research or to the build.

- **Google Tag Manager: cut.** PostHog already does the tracking. GTM would add a second script and a second set of cookies to answer the same question. It comes back if you add a tool that only installs through GTM.

# Scope

The default answer to "should we add this?" is no, until it earns its place. The job is a short, explicit line between what gets built now and what waits.

## Input

An honest brief: options with what each gives, costs, and risks, ideally from j-research's landscape step. If there is none, write a short one from what you know and say it is unresearched. If a research vault is in use, search it for earlier decision pages on the topic and say so if this scope would contradict one.

## Settle facts first

Before asking anything, find out what is already true: read the brief, the code and config, and the vault. Whether something is installed, configured, used, or already decided is a fact to check, not a question. Facts only the user knows (their volume, deadline, constraints) go in one batched question, not one at a time.

## Question the user

Ask with the host's structured question tool (`AskUserQuestion` in Claude Code), up to 4 related decisions per call; otherwise ask in chat with numbered options. Each question:

- is a decision only the user can make (goals, budget, risk, taste);
- offers 2 to 4 options, the recommended one first and marked as recommended, each saying what it costs and what you give up;
- takes a position: say what evidence would change your recommendation;
- comes from the brief's evidence, not from hypotheticals.

Good questions: what is done today without this, and what does that workaround cost (if little, propose not building); what result would prove this works; adopt the existing tool or build; which capability can wait; the budget in money and time; what failure is acceptable in the first version.

For every proposed capability, ask yourself first: what does this give us that we don't already have, and what breaks if we leave it out? If nothing breaks, propose cutting it rather than asking. Push back when the user adds scope too; say plainly when something looks like over-engineering. The exception: an addition that is cheap and changes the outcome a lot gets one question rather than a silent cut.

Budget: about 6 decisions for the whole scope. Stop when the line is drawn, often sooner. Do not interview for completeness; when more decisions seem needed, the scope is too big: split it.

## Output

A scope decision:

- **Goal and proof:** the smallest outcome that shows it works, checked by something other than your or the user's say-so (a test, a user, a number).
- **In:** what gets built now, and whether each part is adopted or built.
- **Out:** what waits, each with the signal that would bring it back.
- **Risks accepted.**
- **Against the recommendation:** each choice the user made against your recommendation, so later results can be judged against it.

Use [the decision template](assets/decision-template.md). If a research vault is in use, record it as a `decision` page there. Then hand it back to j-research for implementation research or to the build.

- **The repo only has three files**, so I can't see where `initAnalytics()` gets called. I'll confirm it actually runs before anything relies on it.

This brief is unresearched; I wrote it from the repo and what I know of PostHog.

## What I'd cut, and why

- **Google Tag Manager: cut.** PostHog already does the tracking. GTM would add a second script and a second set of cookies to answer the same question. It comes back if you add a tool that only installs through GTM.
- **A/B tests of the homepage: cut.** At 40 visits a week, telling a 20% improvement apart from noise would take months. It comes back if traffic reaches a few thousand visits a month.
- **CRM integration: cut.** You're probably tracking tens of applications, which a spreadsheet handles fine. Also, a visit tells you an application link was opened, not who opened it. Recruiters forward CVs, so you'd be filling a CRM with guesses. It comes back if you're managing more applications than a sheet can handle.
- **Custom dashboard: adopt PostHog's instead.** One saved insight, "pageviews broken down by `ref`," is your dashboard and takes about 10 minutes. Building your own only makes sense if PostHog can't show something you need.

## Three decisions only you can make

**1. How should you find out a link was opened?**
- **a) (Recommended)** Check the PostHog insight when you want to know. It's free and you're mostly done already. You lose the instant ping.
- b) A Slack alert on each visit from a tagged link, using PostHog's Slack destination. It's about an hour of setup and needs no code. You give up some calm: alerts can come from bots and link-preview crawlers, so some pings will be false.

I'd switch to (b) if your reaction to an open is time-sensitive, for example following up the same day.

**2. What should the tag look like in the URL?**
- **a) (Recommended)** A short opaque code, like `yoursite.com/?r=k7q2`, with the code-to-company mapping kept in your spreadsheet. Recruiters can see it in the link on your CV, so it shouldn't reveal anything.
- b) A readable tag, like `?ref=acme-backend`. It's easier for you, but recruiters can see you're tracking them, and some find that off-putting.

**3. What do you need from the first version?**
- **a) (Recommended)** "This application link was opened at least once, and when." Accept that forwarded links and crawlers make it approximate.
- b) Reliably separating real people from bots. That means filtering on user agent, a bigger and less certain job.

I checked the repo before asking anything. The core feature mostly exists already.

**What's already in the repo**
- PostHog is installed and running (`src/analytics.ts:4`) with `capture_pageview: true`. Each pageview records the full URL, query string included.
- There's no Google Tag Manager (`README.md:2`).
- Traffic is about **40 visits a week** (`README.md:3`).
- I found no earlier scope decisions and no research brief, so the brief below is my own and unresearched.

**Brief (unresearched)**
A per-application link is your site URL with a tag on the end, like `yoursite.com/?ref=acme-backend-2026-11`. PostHog already records that tag. So the core build is a naming convention, about 5 lines of code to save `ref` on the visitor so later pages are credited to it, and one saved PostHog insight filtered by `ref`. That's roughly an hour of work.

Some limits you should know about:
- An open shows that *someone* used that link. It might be the recruiter, a colleague they forwarded it to, or an ATS preview.
- Ad blockers stop PostHog, so you'll miss some opens.
- If you put the URL in a PDF CV, every copy of that PDF carries the same tag.

**Cuts I'm proposing without asking:**
- **Google Tag Manager:** it would duplicate PostHog and add a second script and possibly a cookie-consent burden, for no new information. It comes back only if you add tools that can only be installed through GTM.
- **Separate dashboard:** a saved PostHog insight ("pageviews by `ref`") does this job. It comes back if you're tracking more than about 30 applications at once and the insight gets hard to read.
- **Homepage A/B tests:** at 40 visits a week, telling apart even a big difference between two versions would take months. You'd be acting on noise. It comes back if traffic goes above about 1,000 visits a week.
- **CRM integration:** you only know the *link* was opened, not who opened it, so a CRM would hold guesses. Storing named people's browsing data also brings GDPR obligations. A column in the spreadsheet where you track applications already does this. It comes back if you're running more than about 50 live applications and the spreadsheet starts slipping.

**Three decisions only you can make.** Reply with something like "1a 2a 3b".

1. **Do you need to know quickly, or is checking enough?**
   - a) **(Recommended)** Check the PostHog insight when you want to know. Costs nothing.
   - b) Send a Slack alert on the first open of each `ref`, using PostHog's Slack destination. About 30 minutes of setup. The catch is noise from previews and repeat opens.

   I'd switch to (b) if you would actually act within hours of an open, for example by sending a follow-up that same day.

2. **Where do your CVs go?**
   - a) **(Recommended)** I make one PDF per application, each with its own link. Works if you send fewer than about 20 applications a month.
   - b) Mostly through ATS portals or LinkedIn Easy Apply. In that case links get stripped or previewed by bots, and the whole feature is worth less. We should talk about that before building anything.

3. **What would show this worked?**
   - a) **(Recommended)** In the next 10 applications, at least one `ref` shows an open in PostHog that you can match to a real application.
   - b) Something else you'd measure.

graders.evidence:
I'd skip Redis for launch. Your API already has a cache, and nothing in the repo shows it falling short.

**What the repo shows:**
- **There's already a cache.** `src/cache.ts:3` keeps an in-memory cache of up to 5,000 entries for 60 seconds in front of the database on read endpoints.
- **The load is light.** `docs/metrics.md` shows a peak of 12 requests/second, with 95% of requests finishing within 48 ms and 81% served from the cache. That's on one app server.
- **Redis would only fix things you don't have yet.** It would let several servers share one cache, keep the cache through restarts, and give you one place to clear stale data. With a single server, none of those is a problem. What you'd take on is a new service to run and pay for, a network hop on every cache read, and a new way for the API to fail.

No research brief existed, so this rests only on the repo. I found no earlier decisions on caching.

I need two things only you know before I finalise this:

1. **What traffic do you expect at launch?**
   - a) **Up to ~10× today (about 120 req/s) (recommended assumption).** One Node server with the current cache should handle this. It costs nothing, but you're trusting that estimate.
   - b) **A big spike (press, Product Hunt, a large customer).** This calls for a load test before launch, not Redis by default.
2. **Will you run more than one API server at launch?**
   - a) **No, one server (recommended).** The current cache is enough.
   - b) **Yes.** Each server would keep its own cache, so data can be stale for up to 60 seconds and the database sees more traffic. Redis starts to make sense here, though the 60-second expiry may be fine anyway.

I'd change my recommendation if you answer 1b and a load test shows the database is the bottleneck, or if you answer 2b and stale data is a real problem for your product.

---

## Draft scope decision: API caching, 2026-11-07

**Goal and proof:** Launch on the current in-memory cache. Proof: after launch, 95% of requests still finish within about 100 ms and the cache hit rate stays above 75%, measured as in `docs/metrics.md`.

**In:**
- **In-memory cache** (adopted, already built): keep it unchanged.
- **Measuring after launch** (built, about an hour of work): make sure hit rate and response time are tracked from launch day.

**Out:**
- **Redis cache:** comes back if you add a second API server, if users report problems from stale data, or if response times climb while the database is maxed out.
- **Load test:** comes back if you expect a big traffic spike (answer 1b).

**Risks accepted:**
- Each restart empties the cache, so the database takes the full load until it refills.
- A sudden spike could hit the database harder than expected.

**Against the recommendation:** none yet.

Answer the two questions and I'll finalise this, or update it if your answers change the picture.

# Scope

The default answer to "should we add this?" is no, until it earns its place. The job is a short, explicit line between what gets built now and what waits.

## Input

An honest brief: options with what each gives, costs, and risks, ideally from j-research's landscape step. If there is none, write a short one from what you know and say it is unresearched. If a research vault is in use, search it for earlier decision pages on the topic and say so if this scope would contradict one.

## Settle facts first

Before asking anything, find out what is already true: read the brief, the code and config, and the vault. Whether something is installed, configured, used, or already decided is a fact to check, not a question. Facts only the user knows (their volume, deadline, constraints) go in one batched question, not one at a time.

## Question the user

Ask with the host's structured question tool (`AskUserQuestion` in Claude Code), up to 4 related decisions per call; otherwise ask in chat with numbered options. Each question:

- is a decision only the user can make (goals, budget, risk, taste);
- offers 2 to 4 options, the recommended one first and marked as recommended, each saying what it costs and what you give up;
- takes a position: say what evidence would change your recommendation;
- comes from the brief's evidence, not from hypotheticals.

Good questions: what is done today without this, and what does that workaround cost (if little, propose not building); what result would prove this works; adopt the existing tool or build; which capability can wait; the budget in money and time; what failure is acceptable in the first version.

For every proposed capability, ask yourself first: what does this give us that we don't already have, and what breaks if we leave it out? If nothing breaks, propose cutting it rather than asking. Push back when the user adds scope too; say plainly when something looks like over-engineering. The exception: an addition that is cheap and changes the outcome a lot gets one question rather than a silent cut.

Budget: about 6 decisions for the whole scope. Stop when the line is drawn, often sooner. Do not interview for completeness; when more decisions seem needed, the scope is too big: split it.

## Output

A scope decision:

- **Goal and proof:** the smallest outcome that shows it works, checked by something other than your or the user's say-so (a test, a user, a number).
- **In:** what gets built now, and whether each part is adopted or built.
- **Out:** what waits, each with the signal that would bring it back.
- **Risks accepted.**
- **Against the recommendation:** each choice the user made against your recommendation, so later results can be judged against it.

Use [the decision template](assets/decision-template.md). If a research vault is in use, record it as a `decision` page there. Then hand it back to j-research for implementation research or to the build.

# Scope

The default answer to "should we add this?" is no, until it earns its place. The job is a short, explicit line between what gets built now and what waits.

## Input

An honest brief: options with what each gives, costs, and risks, ideally from j-research's landscape step. If there is none, write a short one from what you know and say it is unresearched. If a research vault is in use, search it for earlier decision pages on the topic and say so if this scope would contradict one.

## Settle facts first

Before asking anything, find out what is already true: read the brief, the code and config, and the vault. Whether something is installed, configured, used, or already decided is a fact to check, not a question. Facts only the user knows (their volume, deadline, constraints) go in one batched question, not one at a time.

## Question the user

Ask with the host's structured question tool (`AskUserQuestion` in Claude Code), up to 4 related decisions per call; otherwise ask in chat with numbered options. Each question:

- is a decision only the user can make (goals, budget, risk, taste);
- offers 2 to 4 options, the recommended one first and marked as recommended, each saying what it costs and what you give up;
- takes a position: say what evidence would change your recommendation;
- comes from the brief's evidence, not from hypotheticals.

Good questions: what is done today without this, and what does that workaround cost (if little, propose not building); what result would prove this works; adopt the existing tool or build; which capability can wait; the budget in money and time; what failure is acceptable in the first version.

For every proposed capability, ask yourself first: what does this give us that we don't already have, and what breaks if we leave it out? If nothing breaks, propose cutting it rather than asking. Push back when the user adds scope too; say plainly when something looks like over-engineering. The exception: an addition that is cheap and changes the outcome a lot gets one question rather than a silent cut.

Budget: about 6 decisions for the whole scope. Stop when the line is drawn, often sooner. Do not interview for completeness; when more decisions seem needed, the scope is too big: split it.

## Output

A scope decision:

- **Goal and proof:** the smallest outcome that shows it works, checked by something other than your or the user's say-so (a test, a user, a number).
- **In:** what gets built now, and whether each part is adopted or built.
- **Out:** what waits, each with the signal that would bring it back.
- **Risks accepted.**
- **Against the recommendation:** each choice the user made against your recommendation, so later results can be judged against it.

Use [the decision template](assets/decision-template.md). If a research vault is in use, record it as a `decision` page there. Then hand it back to j-research for implementation research or to the build.

graders.evidence:
I checked the repo first. No research vault is in use, so this brief isn't researched and is built only from the code and metrics.

## What I found

- **There's already a cache.** `src/cache.ts:3` puts an in-memory LRU in front of the database for read endpoints (5,000 entries, 60s expiry).
- **Load is low and the cache is working.** `docs/metrics.md:2` covers the last 30 days: peak 12 requests per second, p95 latency 48 ms, cache hit rate 81%.
- **There's one app server.** The README confirms a single Node instance.

## Brief: what Redis would give you

| Option | What you get | Cost | Risk |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A. Keep the in-memory LRU (recommended)** | Nothing new. Current numbers are already fine. | None | Each restart empties the cache, so you get a short burst of database load after deploys |
| B. Replace it with Redis | A cache that survives restarts and can be shared once you run several app servers | Setting up and running Redis, a network hop on every cache read, retry logic, a new way for things to fail at launch | More moving parts right before launch, for a gain the metrics don't show you need |
| C. Leave Redis ready but switched off | Easier move to Redis later | A small abstraction and some config | Small, but it's still work spent before you need it |

**My position:** don't add Redis before launch. It mainly helps when there are several app servers or the cache must survive restarts, and you have neither problem today. At 12 rps with a 48 ms p95, the cache isn't what's holding you back. If you hit limits, the next step is more likely raising `max` or the TTL in `cache.ts`, which is a one-line change.

**What would change my mind:** a plan to run more than one instance at launch; expected launch traffic well above current levels (roughly 10× or more) with the database as the known bottleneck; or reads that must stay consistent across instances.

## Questions only you can answer

1. **How many instances at launch?**
   - a) **One, same as today (recommended).** Redis adds little.
   - b) Two or more behind a load balancer. Each instance keeps its own cache, so hit rates fall and users can see different data on different instances. That's a real reason to consider Redis.
2. **Expected launch traffic compared with today's 12 rps peak?**
   - a) **Under about 10×, around 120 rps or less (recommended to assume unless you have data).** A single instance with the LRU should handle it. Proof is a load test.
   - b) Over 10×, or a known spike such as a press launch. Load-test first, then decide. Redis may still not be the fix.
3. **How bad is a cold cache after a deploy or crash?**
   - a) **Acceptable (recommended).** The database takes misses for about 60s.
   - b) Not acceptable. That favours Redis, or warming the cache on startup, which is cheaper.
4. **How long until launch?**
   - a) **Under 4 weeks (recommended to stay out).** Don't add new infrastructure this close to launch.
   - b) More than 4 weeks. There's room, but the case for Redis still has to come from questions 1–3.

Reply with something like "1a 2a 3a 4a" and I'll write the final scope decision: goal and proof, In, Out with the signals that would bring Redis back, risks accepted, and any choices made against my recommendation.

# Scope

The default answer to "should we add this?" is no, until it earns its place. The job is a short, explicit line between what gets built now and what waits.

## Input

An honest brief: options with what each gives, costs, and risks, ideally from j-research's landscape step. If there is none, write a short one from what you know and say it is unresearched. If a research vault is in use, search it for earlier decision pages on the topic and say so if this scope would contradict one.

## Settle facts first

Before asking anything, find out what is already true: read the brief, the code and config, and the vault. Whether something is installed, configured, used, or already decided is a fact to check, not a question. Facts only the user knows (their volume, deadline, constraints) go in one batched question, not one at a time.

## Question the user

Ask with the host's structured question tool (`AskUserQuestion` in Claude Code), up to 4 related decisions per call; otherwise ask in chat with numbered options. Each question:

- is a decision only the user can make (goals, budget, risk, taste);
- offers 2 to 4 options, the recommended one first and marked as recommended, each saying what it costs and what you give up;
- takes a position: say what evidence would change your recommendation;
- comes from the brief's evidence, not from hypotheticals.

Good questions: what is done today without this, and what does that workaround cost (if little, propose not building); what result would prove this works; adopt the existing tool or build; which capability can wait; the budget in money and time; what failure is acceptable in the first version.

For every proposed capability, ask yourself first: what does this give us that we don't already have, and what breaks if we leave it out? If nothing breaks, propose cutting it rather than asking. Push back when the user adds scope too; say plainly when something looks like over-engineering. The exception: an addition that is cheap and changes the outcome a lot gets one question rather than a silent cut.

Budget: about 6 decisions for the whole scope. Stop when the line is drawn, often sooner. Do not interview for completeness; when more decisions seem needed, the scope is too big: split it.

## Output

A scope decision:

- **Goal and proof:** the smallest outcome that shows it works, checked by something other than your or the user's say-so (a test, a user, a number).
- **In:** what gets built now, and whether each part is adopted or built.
- **Out:** what waits, each with the signal that would bring it back.
- **Risks accepted.**
- **Against the recommendation:** each choice the user made against your recommendation, so later results can be judged against it.

Use [the decision template](assets/decision-template.md). If a research vault is in use, record it as a `decision` page there. Then hand it back to j-research for implementation research or to the build.

Grilling approach adapted from Matt Pocock's [grilling skill](https://github.com/mattpocock/skills); status quo and position-taking from gstack's [office-hours](https://github.com/garrytan/gstack/tree/main/office-hours).

## What I found

- **There's already a cache.** `src/cache.ts:3` puts an in-memory LRU in front of the database for read endpoints (5,000 entries, 60s expiry).
- **Load is low and the cache is working.** `docs/metrics.md:2` covers the last 30 days: peak 12 requests per second, p95 latency 48 ms, cache hit rate 81%.
- **There's one app server.** The README confirms a single Node instance.

## Brief: what Redis would give you

| Option | What you get | Cost | Risk |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A. Keep the in-memory LRU (recommended)** | Nothing new. Current numbers are already fine. | None | Each restart empties the cache, so you get a short burst of database load after deploys |
| B. Replace it with Redis | A cache that survives restarts and can be shared once you run several app servers | Setting up and running Redis, a network hop on every cache read, retry logic, a new way for things to fail at launch | More moving parts right before launch, for a gain the metrics don't show you need |
| C. Leave Redis ready but switched off | Easier move to Redis later | A small abstraction and some config | Small, but it's still work spent before you need it |

**My position:** don't add Redis before launch. It mainly helps when there are several app servers or the cache must survive restarts, and you have neither problem today. At 12 rps with a 48 ms p95, the cache isn't what's holding you back. If you hit limits, the next step is more likely raising `max` or the TTL in `cache.ts`, which is a one-line change.

**What would change my mind:** a plan to run more than one instance at launch; expected launch traffic well above current levels (roughly 10× or more) with the database as the known bottleneck; or reads that must stay consistent across instances.

## Questions only you can answer

1. **How many instances at launch?**
   - a) **One, same as today (recommended).** Redis adds little.
   - b) Two or more behind a load balancer. Each instance keeps its own cache, so hit rates fall and users can see different data on different instances. That's a real reason to consider Redis.
2. **Expected launch traffic compared with today's 12 rps peak?**
   - a) **Under about 10×, around 120 rps or less (recommended to assume unless you have data).** A single instance with the LRU should handle it. Proof is a load test.
   - b) Over 10×, or a known spike such as a press launch. Load-test first, then decide. Redis may still not be the fix.
3. **How bad is a cold cache after a deploy or crash?**

## Brief: what Redis would give you

| Option | What you get | Cost | Risk |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A. Keep the in-memory LRU (recommended)** | Nothing new. Current numbers are already fine. | None | Each restart empties the cache, so you get a short burst of database load after deploys |
| B. Replace it with Redis | A cache that survives restarts and can be shared once you run several app servers | Setting up and running Redis, a network hop on every cache read, retry logic, a new way for things to fail at launch | More moving parts right before launch, for a gain the metrics don't show you need |
| C. Leave Redis ready but switched off | Easier move to Redis later | A small abstraction and some config | Small, but it's still work spent before you need it |

   - a) **Acceptable (recommended).** The database takes misses for about 60s.
   - b) Not acceptable. That favours Redis, or warming the cache on startup, which is cheaper.

   - a) **Under 4 weeks (recommended to stay out).** Don't add new infrastructure this close to launch.

# Scope

The default answer to "should we add this?" is no, until it earns its place. The job is a short, explicit line between what gets built now and what waits.

## Input

An honest brief: options with what each gives, costs, and risks, ideally from j-research's landscape step. If there is none, write a short one from what you know and say it is unresearched. If a research vault is in use, search it for earlier decision pages on the topic and say so if this scope would contradict one.

## Settle facts first

Before asking anything, find out what is already true: read the brief, the code and config, and the vault. Whether something is installed, configured, used, or already decided is a fact to check, not a question. Facts only the user knows (their volume, deadline, constraints) go in one batched question, not one at a time.

## Question the user

Ask with the host's structured question tool (`AskUserQuestion` in Claude Code), up to 4 related decisions per call; otherwise ask in chat with numbered options. Each question:

- is a decision only the user can make (goals, budget, risk, taste);
- offers 2 to 4 options, the recommended one first and marked as recommended, each saying what it costs and what you give up;
- takes a position: say what evidence would change your recommendation;
- comes from the brief's evidence, not from hypotheticals.

Good questions: what is done today without this, and what does that workaround cost (if little, propose not building); what result would prove this works; adopt the existing tool or build; which capability can wait; the budget in money and time; what failure is acceptable in the first version.

For every proposed capability, ask yourself first: what does this give us that we don't already have, and what breaks if we leave it out? If nothing breaks, propose cutting it rather than asking. Push back when the user adds scope too; say plainly when something looks like over-engineering. The exception: an addition that is cheap and changes the outcome a lot gets one question rather than a silent cut.

Budget: about 6 decisions for the whole scope. Stop when the line is drawn, often sooner. Do not interview for completeness; when more decisions seem needed, the scope is too big: split it.

## Output

A scope decision:

- **Goal and proof:** the smallest outcome that shows it works, checked by something other than your or the user's say-so (a test, a user, a number).
- **In:** what gets built now, and whether each part is adopted or built.
- **Out:** what waits, each with the signal that would bring it back.
- **Risks accepted.**
- **Against the recommendation:** each choice the user made against your recommendation, so later results can be judged against it.

Use [the decision template](assets/decision-template.md). If a research vault is in use, record it as a `decision` page there. Then hand it back to j-research for implementation research or to the build.

graders.evidence:
# Redis caching scope, 2026-11-07

**My recommendation: don't add Redis before launch.** The API already has a cache, and nothing in the numbers shows a problem Redis would solve.

There was no research brief for this, so this decision rests only on what's in the repo:
- `src/cache.ts:1-3`: an in-memory LRU cache (`lru-cache`) already sits in front of the database for read endpoints. It holds up to 5,000 entries for 60 seconds each.
- `docs/metrics.md:2`: over the last 30 days, traffic peaked at **12 requests/second**, 95% of requests finished in **48 ms**, the cache answered **81%** of reads, and everything runs on **one app server**.

## What Redis would add, and what breaks without it
Redis does two things the current cache can't:
1. **It shares one cache across several servers.** You run one server, so this doesn't matter yet.
2. **It keeps the cache when the app restarts.** Today a deploy empties the cache, and it fills again within at most 60 seconds. At 12 requests/second that's a small, short spike in database load.

Leaving it out breaks nothing. Adding it means another service to run, monitor and secure, plus a network call on every cache lookup. With a single server, that call can make reads slightly *slower* than the in-memory cache.

## Goal and proof
Reads stay fast at launch traffic. Proof: a load test at your expected launch peak (I'd use 5–10× today's 12 requests/second) keeps 95% of requests under your latency target and doesn't overload the database.

## In
- **Keep the existing in-memory cache** (`lru-cache`, already in use). Don't change it.
- **Run that load test before launch.** This is the cheap check that tells you whether any of this matters.

## Out
- **Redis:** waits. Add it when any of these happens:
  - you run a **second app server** (each server would otherwise keep its own cache, and they'd show different data);
  - the load test shows the **database is the bottleneck** even with the cache in place;
  - **cold-cache spikes after deploys** show up as real errors or slow responses.
- **Tuning the cache size and expiry time:** waits until the load test shows a low cache hit rate.

## Risks accepted
- Each deploy starts with an empty cache, causing up to 60 seconds of extra database reads.
- Moving to several servers will need a shared cache at that point. That's a known follow-up, not a surprise.

## Against the recommendation
None yet.

**One thing only you know, which could change this:** what launch traffic do you expect, and do you plan to run more than one server at launch? If you expect well beyond about 10× today's load, or several servers from day one, Redis comes back into scope. Otherwise this is ready to hand to the build: run the load test and ship as it is.
